Form in Popular Music: Practice for Chapter 12

Hear the forms of Chapter 12 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom played by the site’s backing band: verse–chorus (simple and contrasting), 32-bar AABA and ABAC, the 12-bar blues, and harmonically closed and open sections, with the section shown as it plays and two listening quizzes.

This page goes with Chapter 12, Form in Popular Music of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first. The book draws on John Covach’s essay “Form in Rock Music” and analyses real songs with timings. Here, the site’s backing band plays each form on made-up chord progressions, so you can hear how it is built without a melody or lyrics.

How the demos work: press ▶ Play. The strip at the bottom of the page shows the bar and the section the band is in (“Bar 9 · A2”). Each demo shows its chord grid with the sections labelled, the whole form at once (or one section at a time: pick it above the grid). The bar being played lights up. The buttons change the form; the band starts the new one from bar 1. As soon as the band starts, what it will play the whole way through is written out under the grid, section by section, so you can read ahead. Most forms here are 32 bars, about a minute at this tempo. Listen through at least once.

12.1 Verse–chorus form

The most common form in popular music today. The chorus has the hook, the part everyone remembers. The verses have different words each time and usually a less memorable tune. Songs often add an introduction, a pre-chorus (leading into the chorus), a post-chorus, and a bridge (something new, usually once, late in the song). The book also notes that people disagree about what to call some sections, and that is normal. Read 12.1

The book separates simple verse–chorus form (the verse and chorus use the same chord progression, so only the melody and words tell them apart) from contrasting verse–chorus form (the chorus has its own progression). Here are both, as verse, chorus, verse, chorus:

In the simple form, nothing in the chords tells you where the chorus starts. The singer’s melody and the words would do that, and a band usually plays the chorus fuller and louder. In the contrasting form you can hear the change of progression at bar 9.

12.2 AABA form

The form of Broadway and the Great American Songbook from the 1930s to the 1950s, and of many 1960s songs (the book names “Yesterday” and “Hey Jude”). There are four sections of eight bars. The A section is the main tune and comes three times. B, the bridge or “middle eight”, is the contrast. The whole 32 bars is sometimes called the refrain or chorus, and some songs put a verse in front of it. Read 12.2

Notice where the bridge goes: it leaves C, moves through other keys (E7 to Am, D7 to G), and ends on G7, the V chord. That makes the return of A sound like coming home.

12.3 ABAC form

Also 32 bars of four eight-bar sections, but the A section comes back only once, halfway through. The book’s examples are “White Christmas”, “Someday My Prince Will Come”, “When I Fall in Love” and “Star Dust”. It also notes ABAB′, where the last section starts like B and ends differently. Read 12.3

The first A ends on G7, so it is open and leads on. Only C, the last section, really ends.

12.4 The 12-bar blues

Twelve bars in three lines of four: I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I I. It started in the blues in the early 1900s and was carried into swing (“In the Mood”) and early rock and roll (“Johnny B. Goode”, “Hound Dog”, “Rock Around the Clock”). The book’s table is “Johnny B. Goode”. Read 12.4 · The site’s blues lessons go further: the quick change, turnarounds and the jazz blues.

12.5 Harmonically closed and open sections

A section is closed when it ends on the tonic chord (I) and open when it ends somewhere else, usually V and sometimes IV. Open sections lead on to the next section; closed sections can end the song. Read 12.5

Typical places, from the book:

Form Usually closed Usually open
AABA A sections B (the bridge), ending on V
Verse–chorus the chorus (sometimes) verse, pre-chorus, bridge

The same eight bars, closed and then open. Only the last two bars change:

Quizzes

Open or closed? The band plays one eight-bar section, in different keys, again and again. Does it end on I or not?

Which form? The band plays a whole form, chords only. Listen for what comes back and when, then choose. The section names appear in the strip at the bottom once you have answered.

12.6 Practice: real songs

The book’s exercise asks for a timeline of two songs: when each section starts, what it is, and how many bars it lasts. Its answers are in 12.6. Do the same with any song you know well:

  1. Start a timer with the song. Write the time each time something new starts.
  2. Count bars: count the beats in fours, and add a mark for every 1.
  3. Name each section. Which one has the hook? Which one comes back with the same words? Which comes once?
  4. Mark each section open or closed. Does it end on the home chord?

The site’s Timestamp Notes tool keeps timed notes against a recording, if you want to save your timeline.

NoteFor teachers
  • The band: every demo and quiz runs on the site’s Backing Track band. The progressions are made up for this page, not taken from songs. AABA and ABAC share their bridge so that the only difference is the order of the sections.
  • The quizzes: Open or closed plays one of five eight-bar sections for each answer, in C, G, F, D or A. Which form plays one chart for each form, in C. So once students know the charts, they can recognize them rather than the form. Use it for listening practice, not as a test.
  • Section names: the strip at the bottom shows the section while the band plays (in a quiz, only after the answer).
  • Not here: intros, pre-choruses, post-choruses and codas, and the book’s song timelines (the songs are under copyright). The book’s chapter has no video clips.
  • Not checked by ear: the demos were checked by a test that plays each one and checks the notes are written out. Whether they sound convincing has not been checked by listening.
  • The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
